## Project Overview

A quantitative research study examining the key drivers of student dining satisfaction at **Cal Poly Pomona's** on-campus restaurants.

- 68 survey responses collected
- Factors examined: food quality, cleanliness, price fairness, operational issues, and mobile ordering
- Goal: identify what most significantly affects students' overall dining experience

---

## Tools & Frameworks Used

- **Qualtrics** — survey design & data collection
- **R** — statistical analysis
- **SERVQUAL / RATER Framework** — Parasuraman et al., 1988
- **Theory of Planned Behaviour** — Ajzen, 1991

---

## Research Question

> *What factors (food, service, and operations) affect student satisfaction with Cal Poly Pomona Dining Services?*

---

## Methodology

- **17-question Qualtrics survey** distributed via QR-code flyers and Instagram
- Survey captured dining habits, venue experience, and satisfaction
- Question types: Likert scales, multiple choice, net promoter score, open-ended
- **Sample:** 68 valid responses from students who ate at campus dining venues

---

## Hypotheses Tested

| Hypothesis | Description | Result |
|---|---|---|
| H1 | Operational factors stronger than food/price | ❌ Not Supported |
| H2 | Food quality → higher satisfaction | ✅ Supported |
| H3 | Mobile ordering users → higher satisfaction | ❌ Not Supported |
| H4 | Cleanliness → higher satisfaction | ✅ Supported |

---

## Regression Analysis — H1

**Price vs. Operations on Satisfaction**

- Model significant: F(2, 44) = 11.67, p < .001, R² = .347
- Price fairness: **β = .265, p < .001** ✅ significant
- Operational factors: β = .068, p = .218 ❌ not significant
- **H1 not supported** — price fairness had a stronger impact than operations

---

## Regression Analysis — H2

**Food Quality on Satisfaction**

- Model significant: F(1, 51) = 16.34, p < .001, R² = .243
- Food quality: **β = 0.40, p < .001** ✅ significant
- Students who rated food quality higher reported significantly higher satisfaction
- **H2 supported**

---

## Regression Analysis — H3

**Mobile Ordering on Satisfaction**

- Model not significant: F(1, 47) = 3.23, p = .079, R² = .064
- Mobile ordering: β = 0.21, p = .079 ❌ not significant
- Positive trend but did not meet the α = .05 threshold
- **H3 not supported**

---

## Regression Analysis — H4

**Cleanliness on Satisfaction**

- Model significant: F(1, 51) = 12.67, p = .001, R² = .199
- Cleanliness: **β = 0.34, p = .001** ✅ significant
- Students who rated dining areas as clean reported higher satisfaction
- **H4 supported**

---

## Chi-Square Test

**Campus Presence vs. Satisfaction**

- χ²(4, N = 53) = 5.27, p = .261
- **Not statistically significant**
- How often students are on campus does not meaningfully relate to satisfaction

---

## Cluster Segmentation

| Segment | Share | Profile |
|---|---|---|
| Satisfied Regulars | 35% | High ratings across food, cleanliness, service |
| Value Seekers | 40% | Satisfaction driven by price & portion size |
| Convenience-Driven Strugglers | 25% | Frustrated by wait times, hours, mobile ordering |

---

## Key Findings

- **Food quality & cleanliness** were the strongest drivers of satisfaction
- **Price fairness** mattered more than operational factors
- **Mobile ordering** had no significant effect — lowest-rated attribute
- **Centerpointe Dining** most visited (29 visits), followed by Panda Express & Starbucks (23 each)

---

## Conclusion

Core service attributes — food quality, cleanliness, and price fairness — are the primary drivers of student dining satisfaction at Cal Poly Pomona.

Campus dining services should prioritize:

- Maintaining food quality standards
- Ensuring cleanliness
- Addressing price perception

---

## Limitations

- **Sample size:** 68 respondents via convenience sampling
- **Single institution & timeframe:** One university, one semester
- **Self-report bias:** Recall and social desirability bias possible
- **Measurement depth:** Some constructs captured with too few items
- **Limited qualitative data:** Minimal open-ended responses
